events.enhanced_description: In 1709, the second Eddystone Lighthouse, designed by John Rudyerd, was completed off the southwest coast of England. This lighthouse became a crucial navigation aid for ships in the treacherous waters of the English Channel.

events.name: Publication of De Nostri Temporis Studiorum Ratione
events.enhanced_description: In 1709, Neapolitan philosopher Giambattista Vico published 'De Nostri Temporis Studiorum Ratione' (On the Study Methods of Our Times), contributing to the discourse on education and philosophy in early modern Europe.

events.name: Destruction of medieval altarpieces
events.enhanced_description: In 1709, priceless medieval altarpieces created by Tyrolese sculptor Michael Pacher were destroyed, marking a significant loss in the cultural heritage of the region. This event highlighted the fragility of art during times of conflict.

events.name: Basil Lazarus III becomes Maphrian
events.enhanced_description: In 1709, Basil Lazarus III was appointed as the Syriac Orthodox Maphrian of the East, a significant religious position within the Syriac Orthodox Church. His leadership would influence the church's direction in the following years.

events.name: Merger of Cölln and Alt-Berlin
events.enhanced_description: In 1710, Frederick I merged the towns of Cölln and Alt-Berlin to form the city of Berlin, a pivotal moment in the development of the capital of Prussia. This merger laid the foundation for Berlin's growth into a major European city.

events.name: Escape of Robert Balfour
figures: Robert Balfour, 5th Lord Balfour of Burleigh
events.enhanced_description: On January 4, 1710, Robert Balfour, 5th Lord Balfour of Burleigh, escaped from the Edinburgh Tolbooth just two days before his scheduled execution for murder. He accomplished this daring escape by exchanging clothes with his sister, showcasing the lengths individuals would go to evade justice.

events.name: Abandonment of Mauritius
events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1710, the Dutch abandoned Mauritius, a colony they had established since 1638. This marked a significant shift in colonial power dynamics in the Indian Ocean region.

events.name: Sacheverell riots
events.enhanced_description: The Sacheverell riots began on March 1, 1710, in London, sparked by an attack on a Presbyterian meeting-house in Lincoln's Inn Fields. The riots reflected the intense political and religious tensions of the time, particularly between the High Church and Low Church factions.

events.name: Discovery of the Pillar of the Boatmen

locations.name: Notre-Dame de Paris, Île de la Cité, Paris, France

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1710, during the construction of a crypt under the nave of Notre-Dame de Paris, the ancient Roman Pillar of the Boatmen was discovered. This archaeological find highlighted the historical significance of the site and its connection to ancient Roman Paris.

events.name: Election of Pylyp Orlyk as Hetman
events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1710, Pylyp Orlyk was elected as the Hetman of the Zaporizhian Host, where he immediately issued the Pacts and Constitutions of Rights and Freedoms. This document is considered one of the first constitutional acts in Ukrainian history, asserting the rights of the Cossacks.

events.name: Statute of Anne
events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1710, the Statute of Anne came into effect, marking the world's first copyright legislation. This law established the rights of authors and creators, laying the groundwork for modern copyright law.

events.name: Meeting of Queen Anne and the Four Mohawk Kings
events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1710, Queen Anne of Great Britain met with the Four Mohawk Kings in London. This meeting was significant in establishing diplomatic relations between the British Crown and Native American tribes.

events.name: Thomas Hancorne's Assize Sermon
events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1710, Thomas Hancorne delivered the county of Swansea's assize sermon titled "The right way to honour and happiness," where he articulated his High Church beliefs. This sermon reflected the religious tensions of the period.

events.name: Formation of the South Sea Company
events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1710, the South Sea Company was established in London, England. This company played a significant role in the economic history of Britain, particularly during the South Sea Bubble.

events.name: Battle of Sirhind
events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1710, the Battle of Sirhind occurred, where an army of 70,000 Sikh rebels led by Banda Singh Bahadur defeated a Mughal force of 25,000 commanded by General Wazir Khan, who was killed in the combat. This battle was a pivotal moment in the Sikh struggle against Mughal rule.

events.name: Tuscarora petition
events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1710, the Tuscarora nation sent a petition to the Province of Pennsylvania, protesting the seizure of their lands and the enslavement of their people by citizens of the Province of Carolina. This event highlighted the ongoing conflicts between Native American tribes and colonial settlers.

events.name: Manx coins become legal tender
events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1710, Manx coins were declared legal tender in the Isle of Man. This decision was significant for the economic development of the island and its trade relations.

events.name: Settlement of New Bern

locations.name: New Bern, North Carolina, United States

coordinate_source.cache_key: New Bern, North Carolina, United States

events.enhanced_description: In June 1710, Protestant Swiss and German Palatines, led by Christoph von Graffenried, traveled to Bath County in the Province of Carolina, displacing the native town of Chattoka to found New Bern. This settlement became one of the first significant European communities in North Carolina.

events.name: Battle of Almenar
events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1710, the Battle of Almenar took place in the Iberian theatre of the War of the Spanish Succession. This battle was part of the larger conflict involving multiple European powers vying for control over Spain.

events.name: Relaunch of HMS Vanguard
events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1710, the British Royal Navy's 90-gun ship HMS Vanguard was relaunched from Chatham after being raised and rebuilt following its sinking in the Great Storm of 1703. This event marked a significant moment in naval history for Britain.

events.name: Battle of Saragossa
events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1710, the Battle of Saragossa occurred during the War of the Spanish Succession, where the Spanish-Bourbon army, commanded by the Marquis de Bay, was defeated by the Habsburg forces under Guido Starhemberg. This battle was a crucial moment in the ongoing conflict for control of Spain.

events.name: Gulliver's Travels
events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1710, Jonathan Swift's satirical novel 'Gulliver's Travels' was published, featuring the character Lemuel Gulliver embarking on his fourth and final journey to the Land of the Houyhnhnms. This work is renowned for its critique of human nature and society.

events.name: Capitulation of Livonia
events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1710, the Swedish garrison in Riga capitulated, marking the end of Swedish rule in modern Latvia. This event was a significant turning point in the Great Northern War.

events.name: Start of the Mascate War
events.enhanced_description: In October 1710, the Mascate War, also known as the War of the Peddlers, began between two rival mercantile groups, the Zillioto family and the Astrid family, in colonial Brazil. This conflict highlighted the economic rivalries in the region.

events.name: Battle of Køge Bay
events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1710, the Battle of Køge Bay occurred during the Great Northern War, resulting in an indecisive outcome between Danish and Norwegian forces. This battle was part of the larger conflict affecting Northern Europe.

events.name: Siege of Port Royal
events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1710, British forces under Francis Nicholson successfully conducted the Siege of Port Royal against a French Acadian garrison and the Wabanaki Confederacy. This victory marked the beginning of British control over what would become Nova Scotia.

events.name: First visit to the Pacific islands of Palau
events.enhanced_description: In 1710, a Jesuit expedition led by Francisco Padilla made the first recorded visit to the Pacific islands of Palau. Unfortunately, a storm forced their ship to divert to Mindanao, leaving two priests stranded on the islands.

events.name: Battle of Brihuega
events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1710, during the War of the Spanish Succession, an outnumbered British force under the command of James Stanhope was forced to surrender at the Battle of Brihuega. This defeat significantly impacted the British position in the war.

events.name: Battle of Villaviciosa
events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Villaviciosa, fought on December 10, 1710, was an indecisive engagement between retreating Austrian-Dutch forces and a Franco-Spanish army during the War of the Spanish Succession. The battle highlighted the ongoing struggle for control in the region.

events.name: Battle of Lohgarh
events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Lohgarh took place in 1710 between Sikh forces and the Mughal army. This battle was part of the larger conflict between the Sikhs and the Mughal Empire during the early 18th century.

events.name: Foundation of the Royal Society of Sciences in Uppsala
events.enhanced_description: In 1710, the Royal Society of Sciences was founded in Uppsala, Sweden, originally known as the Collegium curiosorum. This institution played a significant role in the advancement of scientific knowledge in Sweden.

events.name: Juan Arias Diaz visits Choquequirao
events.enhanced_description: In 1710, explorer Juan Arias Diaz became the first non-Incan visitor to Choquequirao, an important Inca archaeological site in Peru. His visit marked a significant moment in the exploration and understanding of Inca history.

events.name: Smithwick's ale brewing begins
events.enhanced_description: In 1710, John Smithwick began brewing Smithwick's ale at St. Francis Abbey Brewery in Kilkenny, Ireland. This brewery would go on to become one of the most famous producers of Irish ale.

events.name: Alexis Littré's treatise on lumbar colostomy
events.enhanced_description: In 1710, Alexis Littré published his treatise 'Diverses observations anatomiques,' where he became the first physician to suggest the possibility of performing a lumbar colostomy for colon obstruction. This marked a significant advancement in surgical practices.

events.name: Jacob Christoph Le Blon's invention
events.enhanced_description: In 1710, Jacob Christoph Le Blon invented a three-color printing process using red, blue, and yellow plates in Amsterdam. This innovation laid the groundwork for the modern CMYK printing process.

events.name: Cary's Rebellion

locations.name: Pamlico River, North Carolina, United States

coordinate_source.cache_key: Pamlico River, North Carolina, United States

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1711, Lieutenant Governor Alexander Spotswood of Virginia sent Royal Marines to assist Governor Hyde during Cary's Rebellion. This rebellion, led by Thomas Cary, was a significant conflict over governance in the Province of Carolina, ultimately leading to Cary's defeat and imprisonment.

events.name: First performance of Tamerlano
events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1711, the first performance of Francesco Gasparini's opera 'Tamerlano' took place at the Teatro San Cassiano in Venice. This opera became one of Gasparini's most renowned works.

events.name: First Mardi Gras parade in America
events.enhanced_description: In February 1711, French settlers at Fort Louis de la Mobile celebrated Mardi Gras by parading a large papier-mâché ox head on a cart, marking the first Mardi Gras parade in America. This event laid the foundation for the rich tradition of Mardi Gras in the region.

events.name: Thomas Cary's attack on Governor Hyde's forces
events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1711, Thomas Cary, having declared himself Governor of North Carolina, led an armed brigantine up the Chowan River to attack Governor Hyde's fortified forces at Colonel Thomas Pollock's plantation. The attack ultimately failed, resulting in a retreat.

events.name: Founding of The Spectator
events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1711, The Spectator was founded in London by Joseph Addison and Richard Steele. This publication played a significant role in shaping public opinion and literary culture in early 18th-century England.

events.name: Rinaldo premieres
events.enhanced_description: In 1711, George Frideric Handel's opera 'Rinaldo,' the first Italian opera written for the London stage, premiered at the Queen's Theatre in Haymarket. This work marked a significant moment in the history of opera in England.

events.name: Rediscovery of Clipperton Island
events.enhanced_description: On April 3, 1711, Frenchmen Martin de Chassiron and Michel Du Bocage rediscovered Clipperton Island, drawing up the first map and claiming the island for France. This event underscored the ongoing European interest in Pacific exploration.

events.name: Collapse of Elgin Cathedral tower
events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1711, the central tower of Elgin Cathedral in northeast Scotland collapsed on Easter Sunday. This event marked a significant moment in the history of the cathedral, which had already suffered from neglect and decay.

events.name: Treaty of the Lutsk
events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1711, the Treaty of the Lutsk was signed in Lutsk, Poland-Lithuania (modern-day Ukraine), establishing a secret agreement between the Tsardom of Russia and the Ottoman Protectorate of Moldavia. This treaty had significant implications for regional power dynamics.

events.name: Death of Joseph I, Holy Roman Emperor
events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1711, Joseph I, Holy Roman Emperor, died, paving the way for his brother Charles VI's succession. This event complicated the ongoing War of the Spanish Succession, as Charles was a key candidate for the Spanish throne.

events.name: Rabid wolf attacks in Roncà
events.enhanced_description: On April 29, 1711, a rabid wolf fatally injured two shepherds in Roncà, North Italy, and attacked livestock. This incident raised concerns about rabies and wildlife safety in the region.

events.name: Publication of An Essay on Criticism
events.enhanced_description: In May 1711, Alexander Pope published his poem 'An Essay on Criticism' in London. This work became one of the most significant pieces of literary criticism of the time, influencing future generations of writers.

events.name: Military blockade of Helsingør
events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1711, Helsingør, Denmark, was placed under military blockade to prevent an outbreak of plague from spreading to Copenhagen. This year, about one-third of Helsingør's population was killed by the disease, highlighting the severity of the epidemic.

events.name: King Louis XIV becomes the longest-reigning monarch
events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1711, King Louis XIV of France surpassed the previous record of 68 years of reign held by K'inich Janaab' Pakal of the Maya civilization, establishing himself as the longest-reigning monarch in history. His reign, which began in 1643, is noted for its absolute monarchy and the cultural flourishing of France.

events.name: Elevation of São Paulo to city status
events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1711, the town of São Paulo in Brazil was officially elevated to city status, marking a significant milestone in its development. This elevation contributed to the growth of São Paulo as a major urban center in Brazil.

events.name: Treaty of the Pruth
events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of the Pruth was signed on July 21, 1711, between the Ottoman Empire and Russia, effectively ending the Pruth River Campaign. This treaty marked a significant moment in the ongoing conflicts between the two empires, with Russia conceding territory and influence.

events.name: Departure of the Zuytdorp
events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1711, the Dutch East India Company trading ship Zuytdorp set sail from the Netherlands on a voyage to Indonesia, carrying freshly minted silver coins. The ship met a tragic fate, as its wreck site remained undiscovered until the mid-20th century.

events.name: Capture of the galleon San Joaquin
events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1711, the Spanish galleon San Joaquin, part of a treasure fleet sailing from Cartagena de Indias to Spain, surrendered after an engagement with five British ships. This event highlighted the ongoing conflicts over trade and treasure during this period.

events.name: Siege of Bouchain
events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1711, John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough, besieged Bouchain with an army of 30,000 during the War of the Spanish Succession. The siege lasted 34 days and marked the last major victory for Churchill in this extensive conflict.

events.name: First horse race at Ascot Racecourse
events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1711, the first horse race was held at the newly founded Ascot Racecourse, which would go on to become one of the leading racecourses in England. This event marked the beginning of a long-standing tradition in British horse racing.

events.name: Tamachi Raisinhji becomes Jam Sahib
events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1711, Tamachi Raisinhji ascended to the position of Jam Sahib, the ruling prince of Nawanagar State in Gujarat, India. His leadership would play a significant role in the region's history.

events.name: Inauguration of the Cathedral of the Assumption
events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1711, the newly constructed Cathedral of the Assumption was inaugurated in Gozo, Malta. This event marked a significant milestone in the religious and architectural history of the island.

events.name: Quebec Expedition disaster
events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1711, the British Quebec Expedition, part of Queen Anne's War, ended in disaster when eight of its ships were wrecked in the Saint Lawrence River, resulting in the drowning of 890 people, mostly soldiers. This event highlighted the perils of military expeditions during this period.

events.name: Royal Charter for the South Sea Company
events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1711, the South Sea Company received a Royal Charter in Britain, marking its official establishment and paving the way for its future role in trade and finance. This company would later become infamous for its speculative bubble.

events.name: Exploration expedition from New Bern

locations.name: New Bern, North Carolina, United States

coordinate_source.cache_key: New Bern, North Carolina, United States

locations.name: Neuse River, North Carolina, United States

coordinate_source.cache_key: Neuse River, North Carolina, United States

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1711, John Lawson and Christoph von Graffenried, along with two African American slaves and two Native Americans, embarked on an exploration expedition from New Bern, North Carolina, traveling north by canoe up the Neuse River. This journey was part of early colonial exploration efforts in the region.

events.name: Capture of Lawson by Tuscarora
events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1711, Tuscarora natives captured John Lawson, Christoph von Graffenried, and their expeditionary party, bringing them to Catechna. This event was part of the larger context of conflict between Native Americans and European settlers.

events.name: Death of John Lawson
events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1711, John Lawson was killed by Tuscarora natives after being captured during an expedition. His death marked a significant moment in the Tuscarora War, which was characterized by violent conflicts between Native Americans and European settlers.

events.name: Sale of Maladzyechna
events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1711, Bishop Bogusław Gosiewski sold the town of Maladzyechna in the Minsk Region of Belarus to the influential Ogiński family. This transaction reflected the shifting power dynamics in the region during this period.

events.name: Beginning of the Tuscarora War

locations.name: Pamlico River, North Carolina, United States

coordinate_source.cache_key: Pamlico River, North Carolina, United States

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1711, the Tuscarora War began when Tuscarora natives, led by Chief Hancock, raided settlements along the south bank of the Pamlico River in North Carolina, resulting in the deaths of around 130 settlers. This conflict would escalate into a prolonged war between the Tuscarora and European settlers.

events.name: Wreck of HMS Feversham
events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1711, HMS Feversham was wrecked on Scaterie Island, Nova Scotia, resulting in the loss of 102 lives. This maritime disaster highlighted the dangers faced by naval vessels during this era.

events.name: Guillottière bridge stampede
events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1711, a tragic stampede on the Guillottière bridge in Lyon, France, resulted in the deaths of 241 people. The chaos ensued when revelers returning from a festival were blocked from crossing, leading to panic and a deadly crush.

events.name: Yostos becomes Emperor of Ethiopia
events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1711, Yostos killed Tewoflos, ascending to the throne as Emperor of Ethiopia. His reign marked a significant period in Ethiopian history, characterized by internal strife and external pressures.

events.name: Establishment of Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts
events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1711, the Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts was established in Brussels, Belgium. This institution would play a crucial role in the development of the arts in the region and influence future generations of artists.

events.name: Fire at Southwell Minster
events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1711, the southwest spire of Southwell Minster in Nottinghamshire was struck by lightning, causing a fire that spread to the nave and tower, destroying roofs, bells, clock, and organ. This event had a lasting impact on the historic church's architecture.

events.name: Sinking of the Liefde
events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1711, the Dutch East India Company ship Liefde ran aground and sank off Out Skerries in Shetland, resulting in the loss of all but one of her 300 crew members. This maritime disaster underscored the dangers of sea travel during this period.

events.name: Battle of Wismar
events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1711, the Battle of Wismar took place during the Great Northern War, resulting in a decisive Danish victory over Swedish forces. This battle was part of the larger conflict that reshaped the balance of power in Northern Europe.

events.name: No Peace Without Spain Amendment Proposal
events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1711, the Earl of Nottingham successfully proposed the 'No Peace Without Spain' amendment in the Parliament of Great Britain, reflecting the ongoing tensions of the War of the Spanish Succession and the desire to maintain British interests in the region.

events.name: Inauguration of Immaculate Conception Cathedral
events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1711, the Immaculate Conception Cathedral in Comayagua, Honduras, was inaugurated. This cathedral is one of the oldest in Central America and serves as a significant religious site in the region.

events.name: Constitution Approval for Academy of Sciences of Bologna
events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1711, a constitution was approved for the Academy of Sciences of the Institute of Bologna, which had been founded in 1690. This institution played a crucial role in the advancement of scientific knowledge in Italy.

events.name: Establishment of Slave Market on Wall Street
events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1711, Wall Street in New York City became the first official slave market for the sale and rental of enslaved Africans and Indians, marking a significant and troubling chapter in American history regarding slavery and commerce.

events.name: Consecration of the Old Pummerin Bell
figures: Bishop Franz Ferdinand Freiherr von Rummel
events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1711, the Old Pummerin, a massive bell cast from 208 captured cannons, was consecrated by Bishop Franz Ferdinand Freiherr von Rummel in preparation for its installation in St. Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna.

events.name: Completion of St Paul's Cathedral
events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1711, the rebuilding of St Paul's Cathedral in London, designed by Sir Christopher Wren, was declared complete by Parliament. The original cathedral had been destroyed in the Great Fire of London in 1666.

events.name: Woodes Rogers Returns to England
events.enhanced_description: In 1711, Woodes Rogers returned to England after a successful round-the-world privateering cruise against Spain, bringing back loot worth £150,000, showcasing the lucrative nature of privateering during this period.

events.name: Invention of the Tuning Fork
events.enhanced_description: In 1711, John Shore invented the tuning fork, a significant advancement in the field of music and acoustics, allowing for more precise tuning of musical instruments.

events.name: Marsili's Discovery about Coral
events.enhanced_description: In 1711, Luigi Ferdinando Marsili demonstrated that coral is an animal rather than a plant, challenging previous misconceptions and contributing to the field of marine biology.

events.name: Total Solar Eclipse
events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 2017, a total solar eclipse, known as 'The Great American Eclipse', was visible across a band stretching from the Pacific to the Atlantic coasts of the contiguous United States. This astronomical event captivated millions of viewers and was notable for its path of totality.

events.name: Premiere of Idoménée Opera
events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1712, the opera Idoménée by André Campra premiered at the Théâtre du Palais-Royal in Paris, marking a significant event in the French operatic tradition.

events.name: Establishment of Military Engineering School
events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 1712, a military engineering school was established in Moscow, which would later evolve into the A.F. Mozhaysky Military-Space Academy, contributing to military education in Russia.

events.name: First Ringing of the Old Pummerin Bell
events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1712, the Old Pummerin bell, weighing 18,161 kg, was rung for the first time at St. Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna to mark the entry of Charles VI into the city after his coronation as Emperor.

events.name: Huilliche Uprising of 1712
events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1712, the Huilliche people in Chile's Chiloé Archipelago rose up against Spanish encomenderos in a rebellion fueled by grievances over injustices, marking a significant indigenous resistance against colonial rule.

events.name: Start of the Cassard Expedition
events.enhanced_description: In early March 1712, French Navy captain Jacques Cassard began his expedition, during which he ransacked Santiago in the Cape Verde Islands and pillaged several Caribbean islands, returning to France with loot valued at over nine million francs.

events.name: Scottish Episcopalians Act 1711
events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1712, the Scottish Episcopalians Act 1711 came into effect, leading to the incorporation of the Scottish Episcopal Church, a significant development in the religious landscape of Scotland.

events.name: Sweden Adopts February 30
events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1712, Sweden temporarily adopted the rare February 30 as a day to adjust the Swedish Calendar back to the Julian calendar, a unique occurrence in the history of timekeeping.

events.name: Wreck of HMS Dragon
events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1712, HMS Dragon, a 38-gun fourth-rate frigate of the British Royal Navy, was wrecked on Les Casquets rocks to the west of Alderney, highlighting the perils faced by naval vessels of the time.

events.name: Queen Anne's Last Royal Touch
events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1712, Queen Anne of Great Britain administered the Royal touch for the last time, touching 300 scrofulous individuals, including the notable Samuel Johnson, in a ritual believed to cure illness.

events.name: New York Slave Revolt of 1712
events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1712, the New York Slave Revolt erupted, resulting in the deaths of nine whites and the execution of 21 slaves and other blacks, marking a significant moment in the history of slavery in the American colonies.

events.name: Battle of Fladstrand
events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1712, the Battle of Fladstrand took place at sea near Fladstrand, Jutland, between Swedish and Danish forces during the Great Northern War, illustrating the ongoing conflict in the region.

events.name: Founding of Curuguaty
figures: Juan Gregorio de Bazán y Pedraza
events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1712, Curuguaty was founded by Juan Gregorio de Bazán y Pedraza on the banks of the Curuguaty River, contributing to the settlement and development of the region in Paraguay.

events.name: Peter the Great Moves Capital
events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1712, Peter the Great moved the capital of Russia from Moscow to Saint Petersburg, a strategic decision that aimed to modernize the Russian state and enhance its maritime capabilities.

events.name: Charles VI Crowned King of Hungary
events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1712, Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor, was crowned King of Hungary, solidifying his rule and influence in Central Europe during a period of political complexity.

events.name: Reus is given the title of imperial city
events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1712, Reus was granted the title of imperial city by Elisabeth Christine, the wife of Archduke Charles, reflecting its importance in the region during the early 18th century.

events.name: Restoration of Kurtkulağı Caravanserai
events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1712, the Kurtkulağı Caravanserai in Adana Province was restored, and 50 soldiers were appointed to guard it, highlighting the importance of caravanserais as safe havens for travelers and merchants in the Ottoman Empire.

events.name: Incorporation of Chatham as a town

locations.name: Chatham, Barnstable County, Massachusetts, United States

coordinate_source.cache_key: Chatham, Barnstable County, Massachusetts, United States

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1712, Chatham was officially incorporated as a town in Barnstable County, Massachusetts, marking its development as a significant community in the region.

events.name: Consecration of St Ann's Church
events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1712, St Ann's Church in Manchester was consecrated by the Bishop of Chester, symbolizing the growth of the Anglican Church in the rapidly industrializing city.

events.name: Launch of HMS Advice
events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1712, the British Royal Navy launched the 50-gun ship HMS Advice at Deptford Dockyard, contributing to the naval power of Great Britain during the early 18th century.

events.name: Death of Jonathan Edwards
events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1712, Jesus College, Oxford inherited the extensive library of its Principal, Jonathan Edwards, upon his death, enriching the academic resources of the institution.

events.name: Battle of Denain
events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1712, during the War of the Spanish Succession, the French forces, led by the Duke of Villars, achieved a decisive victory against a combined Dutch-Austrian army at the Battle of Denain.

events.name: Passage of the Stamp Act 1712
events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1712, the Stamp Act was passed in the United Kingdom, imposing a tax on publishers, particularly targeting newspapers, which would later contribute to tensions leading to the American Revolution.

events.name: Signing of the Peace of Aarau
events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1712, the Peace of Aarau was signed, concluding the Toggenburg War and establishing Protestant dominance in Switzerland while ensuring the rights of Catholics.

events.name: Launch of HMS Rippon
events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1712, the British Royal Navy launched the 60-gun ship HMS Rippon at Deptford Dockyard, further enhancing the naval capabilities of Great Britain.

events.name: George Frideric Handel relocates to London
events.enhanced_description: In September 1712, composer George Frideric Handel relocated to London with the permission of his patron, the future King George I, marking a significant step in his career and influence in English music.

events.name: Hurricane in Bermuda
events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1712, a severe hurricane struck Bermuda, lasting for eight hours and causing extensive damage to most of the churches on the island.

events.name: Battle of Villmergen
events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Villmergen occurred in 1712, where the Reformed cantons of Switzerland defeated the Catholic cantons, further entrenching the religious divisions in the region.

events.name: Warrant for Rob Roy MacGregor's arrest
events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1712, a warrant was issued for the arrest of the notorious outlaw Rob Roy MacGregor by Sir James Stewart, the Lord Advocate of Scotland, reflecting the ongoing tensions between the Scottish clans and the government.

events.name: Establishment of the Biblioteca Nacional de España
events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1712, King Philip V of Spain established the Biblioteca Nacional de España as the Palace Public Library in Madrid, laying the foundation for one of the most important cultural institutions in the country.

events.name: The Bandbox Plot
events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1712, the Bandbox Plot was foiled, which aimed to assassinate British Lord Treasurer Robert Harley, Earl of Oxford, with the intervention of Jonathan Swift, the author of 'Gulliver's Travels'.

events.name: First performance of Il pastor fido
events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1712, the first performance of George Frideric Handel's opera 'Il pastor fido' took place at the Queen's Theatre in the Haymarket, London, marking a significant moment in the history of English opera.

events.name: Charter of Buchach Monastery signed
events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1712, the charter for Buchach Monastery, founded by Stefan Aleksander Potocki and his wife Joanna Sieniawska, was signed in Lublin, establishing a significant religious institution in Ukraine.

events.name: Battle of Gadebusch
events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1712, the Battle of Gadebusch marked Sweden's final significant victory in the Great Northern War, preventing the loss of Stralsund to Danish and Saxon forces.

events.name: Premiere of Callirhoé
events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1712, the opera 'Callirhoé' by André Cardinal Destouches premiered at the Théâtre du Palais-Royal in Paris, showcasing the flourishing French opera scene of the time.

events.name: First working Newcomen steam engine built
events.enhanced_description: In 1712, Thomas Newcomen and John Calley built the first known working steam engine in the Black Country of England, marking a pivotal moment in the Industrial Revolution by making practical use of steam power for mechanical work.

events.name: Establishment of Town on Queen Anne's Creek
events.enhanced_description: In 1712, after years of settlement, the Town on Queen Anne's Creek was established as a courthouse for Chowan County, North Carolina, later renamed Edenton in 1720.

events.name: Wreck of the VOC Zuytdorp
events.enhanced_description: In 1712, the VOC Zuytdorp was wrecked off the coast of Western Australia, a significant maritime disaster during the Dutch East India Company's trading activities.

events.name: John Arbuthnot creates the character of John Bull to represent Britain
events.enhanced_description: In 1712, John Arbuthnot introduced the character of John Bull in his satirical writings, embodying the spirit of Britain as a stout, honest, and somewhat bumbling figure. This character became a national personification of England and has been used in various political cartoons and literature ever since.

events.name: A translation of the 1662 Book of Common Prayer into Irish is published
events.enhanced_description: In 1712, John Richardson published a translation of the 1662 Book of Common Prayer into Irish, making the Anglican liturgy accessible to Irish speakers. This translation played a significant role in the religious and cultural life of Ireland, particularly among the Anglican community.

events.name: Tuscarora War: Colonel James Moore leads the Carolina militia out of Albemarle County, North Carolina

locations.name: Albemarle County, North Carolina, United States

coordinate_source.cache_key: Albemarle County, North Carolina, United States

locations.name: Pamlico River, North Carolina, United States

coordinate_source.cache_key: Pamlico River, North Carolina, United States

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1713, Colonel James Moore led the Carolina militia from Albemarle County in a second offensive against the Tuscarora tribe during the Tuscarora War. Heavy snow forced the troops to take refuge in Fort Reading along the Pamlico River, highlighting the harsh conditions faced by the militia.

events.name: Skirmish at Bender, Moldova: Charles XII of Sweden is defeated by the Ottoman Empire
events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1713, during the Great Northern War, Charles XII of Sweden faced defeat at the Skirmish at Bender against the Ottoman Empire. This battle marked a significant setback for Sweden as it struggled to maintain its influence in Eastern Europe.

events.name: Tuscarora War: The Carolina militia under Colonel James Moore leaves Fort Reading

locations.name: Fort Reading, North Carolina, United States

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1713, Colonel James Moore's Carolina militia departed from Fort Reading to continue their campaign against the Tuscarora tribe during the ongoing Tuscarora War. This movement was part of a larger effort to subdue the Native American resistance in the region.

events.name: Frederick William I of Prussia begins his reign
events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1713, Frederick William I ascended to the throne of Prussia, marking the beginning of his reign. Known as the 'Soldier King,' he focused on military reforms and strengthening the Prussian state.

events.name: Tuscarora War: Colonel James Moore's Carolina militia lays siege to Fort Neoheroka

locations.name: Fort Neoheroka, North Carolina, United States

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1713, Colonel James Moore's Carolina militia laid siege to Fort Neoheroka, a stronghold of the Tuscarora tribe. This action was a crucial part of the military campaign aimed at dismantling the Tuscarora's resistance in North Carolina.

events.name: Tuscarora War: Colonel James Moore's Carolina militia launches a major offensive against Fort Neoheroka

locations.name: Fort Neoheroka, North Carolina, United States

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1713, Colonel James Moore's Carolina militia launched a significant offensive against Fort Neoheroka, intensifying the conflict during the Tuscarora War. This assault was part of a broader strategy to eliminate the Tuscarora threat in the region.

events.name: Tuscarora War: Fort Neoheroka falls to the Carolina militia

locations.name: Fort Neoheroka, North Carolina, United States

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1713, Fort Neoheroka fell to the Carolina militia, effectively ending the military strength of the Tuscarora nation. This victory marked a turning point in the Tuscarora War, although some Tuscaroran allies continued to resist.

events.name: First Treaty of Utrecht between Great Britain and Spain
events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1713, the First Treaty of Utrecht was signed, recognizing Philip V as the king of Spain by Great Britain and Austria. This treaty also resulted in Spain ceding Gibraltar and Menorca to Britain, reshaping the balance of power in Europe.

events.name: The Second Treaty of Utrecht between Great Britain and France ends the War of the Spanish Succession
events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1713, the Second Treaty of Utrecht was signed, officially ending the War of the Spanish Succession. This treaty resulted in France ceding Newfoundland, Acadia, Hudson Bay, and St Kitts to Great Britain, significantly altering colonial territories.

events.name: First performance of Joseph Addison's play Cato, a Tragedy in London
events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1713, Joseph Addison's play 'Cato, a Tragedy' premiered in London. The play, which championed liberty and republicanism, became influential in both British and American political thought.

events.name: Charles VI issues the Pragmatic Sanction of 1713
events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1713, Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor, issued the Pragmatic Sanction, which aimed to ensure that one of his daughters would inherit the Habsburg lands. This decree was crucial for the future of the Habsburg dynasty and European politics.

events.name: Asiento de Negros agreement with Anne, Queen of Great Britain
events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1713, as part of the Treaty of Utrecht, the Spanish Crown agreed to the Asiento de Negros with Anne, Queen of Great Britain. This agreement granted a subsidiary of the British South Sea Company a 30-year monopoly on the supply of African slaves to colonial Spanish America.

events.name: Great Northern War: Russian Navy attacks Swedish Army at Helsinki
events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1713, during the Great Northern War, a fleet of the Russian Navy, carrying 12,000 soldiers, set sail from Kronstadt to attack the Swedish Army stationed at Helsinki. This military action was part of Russia's broader strategy to expand its influence in the Baltic region.

events.name: The Parliament of Ireland is dissolved by Queen Anne
events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1713, Queen Anne dissolved the Parliament of Ireland, setting the stage for new elections. This action reflected the ongoing tensions and political maneuvering between the British crown and Irish governance.

events.name: King Philip V of Spain issues an auto accordado changing succession order
events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1713, King Philip V of Spain issued an auto accordado that altered the order of succession for the Spanish throne, allowing a female descendant within the House of Bourbon to rule. This decision would eventually enable his great-great-granddaughter to ascend the throne as Queen Isabella II in 1833.

events.name: Ottone in villa, the first opera by Antonio Vivaldi, is performed
events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1713, 'Ottone in villa,' the first opera composed by Antonio Vivaldi, premiered at the Teatro delle Grazie in Vicenza. This work marked Vivaldi's entry into the operatic genre and showcased his innovative musical style.

events.name: Great Northern War: Russian fleet lands troops at Pernå
events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1713, during the Great Northern War, the Russian fleet successfully landed a force of 10,000 men at Pernå on the southern coast of Finland. This strategic move was part of Russia's campaign against Sweden.

events.name: Tuscarora War: Colonel James Moore leads the Carolina militia into the Pamlico Peninsula

locations.name: Pamlico Peninsula, North Carolina, United States

events.enhanced_description: In June 1713, Colonel James Moore led the Carolina militia into the Pamlico Peninsula to confront the Machapunga and Coree tribes during the Tuscarora War. This campaign aimed to suppress Native American resistance in the region.

events.name: French residents of Acadia are given one year to declare allegiance to Great Britain
events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1713, French residents of Acadia were given one year to declare their allegiance to Great Britain or face expulsion from Nova Scotia. This ultimatum was part of the broader consequences of the Treaty of Utrecht and the shifting political landscape in North America.

events.name: The Junta de Braços of Catalonia votes to continue the War of the Spanish Succession
events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1713, the Junta de Braços, the parliament of the Principality of Catalonia, voted in favor of continuing the War of the Spanish Succession against Philip V of Spain. This decision reflected the ongoing resistance to Bourbon rule in Catalonia.

events.name: The Treaty of Portsmouth brings an end to Queen Anne's War
events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1713, the Treaty of Portsmouth was signed, officially ending Queen Anne's War. This treaty concluded hostilities between Great Britain and France in North America, reshaping territorial claims in the region.

events.name: The Parliament of Great Britain is dissolved
events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1713, the Parliament of Great Britain, the third since the Act of Union, was dissolved. This dissolution set the stage for new elections and reflected the ongoing political changes in Britain following the conclusion of the War of the Spanish Succession.

events.name: Voting begins in the 1713 British general election
events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1713, voting commenced in the British general election, which would continue until November 12. This election was significant in shaping the political landscape of Great Britain following the end of the War of the Spanish Succession.

events.name: Tuscarora War
events.enhanced_description: The Tuscarora War was a conflict between the Tuscarora Native Americans and European settlers in North Carolina, which saw the Carolina militia, led by Colonel James Moore, return to South Carolina after a campaign against the Machapunga and Coree tribes. The war highlighted the tensions between indigenous peoples and colonial expansion in the early 18th century.

events.name: Treaty of Schwedt
events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Schwedt was a significant agreement signed between Russia and Brandenburg-Prussia, where Brandenburg accepted the annexation of Baltic territories by Russia in exchange for the southern part of Pomerania. This treaty was a key outcome of the Great Northern War, reshaping the balance of power in Northern Europe.

events.name: Battle of Pälkäne
events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Pälkäne was fought between Russian and Swedish forces during the Great Northern War, where Russian commander Fyodor Arpaskin successfully forced the Finnish troops under Carl Gustaf Armfeldt to withdraw. This battle exemplified the ongoing military struggles between the two empires in the region.

events.name: Dublin election riot
events.enhanced_description: The Dublin election riot erupted during the fiercely contested Irish General Election of 1713, reflecting the intense political divisions and social tensions of the time. This riot underscored the volatile nature of electoral politics in early 18th-century Ireland.

events.name: 1713 British general election
events.enhanced_description: The 1713 British general election concluded with the conservative Tory party winning a significant majority in the House of Commons, securing 358 out of 558 seats. This election marked a pivotal moment in British politics, influencing the direction of government and policy in the years to come.

events.name: Treaty of Commerce and Navigation
events.enhanced_description: As part of the agreements made at the Treaty of Utrecht, Great Britain and Spain signed a treaty of commerce and navigation, which aimed to regulate trade relations and facilitate economic exchanges between the two nations. This treaty was a crucial step in stabilizing post-war relations following the War of the Spanish Succession.

events.name: Rebellion of Richard Raworth

locations.name: Fort St. David, Tamil Nadu, India

events.enhanced_description: The rebellion of Richard Raworth, Deputy Governor of Fort St. David, against the British East India Company came to an end after two months when forces sent by Governor Edward Harrison negotiated a settlement. This event highlighted the tensions between colonial authorities and local governance in India.

events.name: Coronation of Victor Amadeus
events.enhanced_description: Victor Amadeus II, Duke of Savoy, was crowned King of Sicily in a ceremony held in Palermo, alongside his wife Anne Marie as Queen consort. This coronation followed Spain's recognition of Sicilian independence, marking a significant moment in the region's political landscape.

events.name: Publication of Ars Conjectandi
events.enhanced_description: Ars Conjectandi, a seminal work on probability theory by Jacob Bernoulli, was published posthumously by his nephew Niklaus Bernoulli. This publication laid foundational principles for the field of probability and statistics, influencing future generations of mathematicians.

events.name: Basil Matthew II becomes Maphrian
events.enhanced_description: Basil Matthew II was appointed as the Syriac Orthodox Maphrian of the East, a significant ecclesiastical position within the Syriac Orthodox Church. His leadership played a crucial role in the church's governance and spiritual guidance during a period of religious and political challenges.

events.name: San Basilio de Palenque becomes free town

locations.name: San Basilio de Palenque, Bolívar, Colombia

coordinate_source.cache_key: San Basilio de Palenque, Bolívar, Colombia

events.enhanced_description: San Basilio de Palenque officially became the first free African town in America, marking a significant milestone in the history of African resistance against colonial rule. This community was established by escaped slaves and became a symbol of freedom and cultural identity.

events.name: Blinding of Azz-ud-din Mirza
events.enhanced_description: Prince Azz-ud-din Mirza was blinded on the orders of Emperor Farrukhsiyar after being tricked into deserting a battle against the Mughal Empire by the rebel Sayyid brothers. This event reflects the internal power struggles and brutal political maneuvers characteristic of the Mughal court.

events.name: Siege of Tönning
events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Tönning concluded after Danish forces compelled the surrender of the remaining defenders, marking a significant victory in the ongoing conflicts of the Great Northern War. The fortress was subsequently leveled by the Danes, symbolizing their dominance in the region.

events.name: Decree on Compulsory Education
events.enhanced_description: Tsar Peter the Great issued a decree mandating compulsory education in mathematics for children of government officials and nobility, targeting those aged 10 to 15 years. This initiative aimed to modernize Russia and improve the educational standards of its ruling class.

events.name: Battle of Storkyro
events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Storkyro was fought between Swedish and Russian forces, resulting in heavy casualties for the outnumbered Swedish troops. This battle was part of the larger conflict of the Great Northern War, showcasing the fierce military engagements between the two empires.

events.name: Treaty of Rastatt
events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Rastatt was signed between Austria and France, concluding the War of the Spanish Succession. This treaty resulted in significant territorial gains for Austria, marking the peak of Habsburg power in Europe.

events.name: France signs treaties to end hostilities
events.enhanced_description: France signed five separate treaties with various nations, including Great Britain and the Netherlands, to formally end hostilities following the War of the Spanish Succession. This series of agreements marked a significant step towards peace in Europe.

events.name: Niccolò Gianpriamo's evangelical trip
events.enhanced_description: Italian Jesuit missionary Niccolò Gianpriamo was dispatched from Portugal on an evangelical mission to Asia, beginning with the Portuguese colony of Goa. His journey highlights the efforts of European missionaries to spread Christianity in Asia during this period.

events.name: Anne refuses House of Hanover
events.enhanced_description: Queen Anne of Great Britain made the controversial decision to refuse permission for members of the House of Hanover to settle in Britain during her lifetime, reflecting the political tensions and succession issues of the time. This decision had lasting implications for the British monarchy.

events.name: Bach's cantata performance
events.enhanced_description: Johann Sebastian Bach led the first performance of his cantata for Pentecost, Erschallet, ihr Lieder, BWV 172, at the chapel of Schloss Weimar. This event marked an important moment in the development of Bach's musical legacy and the cultural life of Weimar.

events.name: Inauguration of water stairs in Kassel
events.enhanced_description: The city of Kassel inaugurated the summer tradition of the "water stairs" or "great cascades" (Grossen Kaskaden), which empty from the base of the Hercules monument down to the Wilhelmshöhe castle. This event marked the beginning of a cultural and artistic tradition that continues to attract visitors.

events.name: Condemnation of papal bull Unigenitus
events.enhanced_description: In France, Bishop Henri-Charles du Cambout de Coislin condemned the papal bull Unigenitus, issued by Pope Clement XI, which inflamed the Jansenist controversy. This condemnation highlighted the ongoing religious tensions within the Catholic Church and the broader society.

events.name: Peace treaty between Spain and the Netherlands
events.enhanced_description: Spain and the Netherlands signed a peace treaty to formally end hostilities between the two nations following the War of the Spanish Succession. This treaty was part of the broader efforts to stabilize Europe after years of conflict.

events.name: Longitude prize vote
events.enhanced_description: The Parliament of Great Britain voted to offer a reward for discovering a method to determine a ship's longitude, with escalating prizes for varying degrees of accuracy. This initiative was crucial for maritime navigation and spurred advancements in scientific understanding.

events.name: Battle of Gangut
events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Gangut marked the first significant naval victory for the Imperial Russian Navy against the Swedish Navy during the Great Northern War. This victory was pivotal in establishing Russian naval power in the Baltic Sea.

events.name: Georg Ludwig von Braunschweig-Lüneburg becomes King George I of Great Britain and Ireland
events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1714, Georg Ludwig von Braunschweig-Lüneburg ascended to the throne as King George I of Great Britain and Ireland following the death of Queen Anne. His accession marked the end of the House of Stuart's reign and the beginning of the House of Hanover, as he was the closest Protestant relative to Anne.

events.name: Barcelona taken during the War of the Spanish Succession
events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1714, after a prolonged siege, Barcelona fell to the Spanish and French Bourbon armies during the War of the Spanish Succession. This event marked a significant turning point in the conflict, leading to the consolidation of Bourbon rule in Spain.

events.name: George I arrives in Britain
events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1714, King George I of Great Britain and Ireland arrived in London for the first time, having sailed from the Netherlands after his accession to the throne. His arrival marked the beginning of a new era in British monarchy under the House of Hanover.

events.name: The Great Hatred on Hailuoto
events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1714, the Cossacks of the Russian Empire perpetrated a massacre on the Finnish island of Hailuoto, killing approximately 800 people overnight. This event is part of the broader context of conflicts involving the Russian Empire during this period.

events.name: Coronation of George I

locations.name: Westminster Abbey, London, England, United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1714, George I was crowned in Westminster Abbey, marking his formal acceptance as the monarch of Great Britain and Ireland. This event solidified his rule and the transition of power from the House of Stuart to the House of Hanover.

events.name: Purchase of Berbice
events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1714, Dutch investors led by brothers Nicolaas and Hendrik van Hoorn purchased the South American colony of Berbice from French mercenary Jacques Cassard. This acquisition played a significant role in the colonial dynamics of the region.

events.name: Reorganization of the Spanish government
events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1714, King Philip V of Spain issued a decree to reorganize the Spanish government, establishing four ministries with the Secretary of State as the chief minister. This marked a significant step towards modernizing the Spanish administration.

events.name: Ottoman Empire declares war on Venice
events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1714, the Ottoman Empire declared war on the Republic of Venice, initiating hostilities that would last until 1718. This conflict was part of the larger struggle for control over territories in the Mediterranean.

events.name: Establishment of Archbishop Tenison's School

locations.name: Croydon, Greater London, England, United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: In 1714, Archbishop Thomas Tenison established Archbishop Tenison's School in Croydon, which is recognized as the world's earliest surviving mixed-gender school. This institution played a crucial role in the evolution of education in England.

events.name: Establishment of Fort St. Jean Baptiste
events.enhanced_description: In 1714, Louis Juchereau de St. Denis established Fort St. Jean Baptiste at the site of present-day Natchitoches, Louisiana. This fort marked the first permanent European settlement in the Louisiana Territory, contributing to the French colonial presence in North America.

events.name: Founding of Worcester College, University of Oxford
events.enhanced_description: In 1714, Worcester College was founded at the University of Oxford, succeeding the earlier Gloucester College, which had been closed during the Dissolution of the Monasteries. This institution continues to be an integral part of Oxford's educational landscape.

events.name: Foundation of Stockholm County
events.enhanced_description: In 1714, Stockholm County was officially founded, establishing a key administrative region in Sweden. This development played a significant role in the governance and organization of the area surrounding the capital.

events.name: Redirection of the Kander River
events.enhanced_description: In 1714, the Kander River in Switzerland was redirected into Lake Thun, a significant engineering project that altered the local landscape and water management. This project reflects the early efforts in hydraulic engineering in the region.

events.name: Fire in London
events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1715, a devastating fire broke out in London, described as the worst since the Great Fire of 1666. The fire started on Thames Street and consumed over 100 houses before it was brought under control.

events.name: Voting begins for the British House of Commons
events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1715, voting commenced for the British House of Commons, continuing for 46 days across various constituencies. This election was significant in shaping the political landscape of Britain.

events.name: Peace treaty ends the Tuscarora War

locations.name: Lake Mattamuskeet, North Carolina, United States

coordinate_source.cache_key: Lake Mattamuskeet, North Carolina, United States

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1715, the Tuscarora and their allies signed a peace treaty with the Province of North Carolina, agreeing to relocate to a reservation near Lake Mattamuskeet. This treaty effectively ended the Tuscarora War, which had significant implications for Native American relations in the region.

events.name: Voting for the British House of Commons concludes
events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1715, voting for the British House of Commons concluded, resulting in a significant victory for the Whig Party, which won 341 out of 558 seats. This election marked a pivotal moment in British political history.

events.name: James Stuart meets Pope Clement XI
events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1715, James Stuart, known as the Old Pretender, met with Pope Clement XI to seek support for his claim to the British throne. This meeting was part of his efforts to restore the House of Stuart to power during the Jacobite rising.

events.name: Henry St John flees to France
events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1715, Henry St John, 1st Viscount Bolingbroke, fled from Great Britain to France due to suspicions regarding his involvement in secret negotiations with France. His departure marked a significant moment in the political turmoil of the time.

events.name: Battle of Gurdas Nangal begins
events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1715, the Battle of Gurdas Nangal commenced during the Mughal-Sikh Wars, as the Mughal Army laid siege to a fortress near Gurdaspur where Sikh General Banda Singh Bahadur and his men were holed up. This battle was part of the larger conflict between the Mughal Empire and the Sikh forces.

events.name: Yamasee Confederation attacks English settlements
events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1715, the Yamasee Confederation launched a surprise attack on English settlements in the Province of South Carolina, marking the beginning of the Yamasee War. This conflict arose from tensions over land and trade between Native Americans and European settlers.

events.name: Battle of Fehmarn
events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1715, the Battle of Fehmarn took place in the Baltic Sea during the Great Northern War, where Danish forces under Christian Gabel captured five Swedish warships. This battle highlighted the naval conflicts between Denmark and Sweden during this period.

events.name: Total solar eclipse observed
events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1715, a total solar eclipse was observed across southern England, Sweden, and Finland, with astronomer Edmond Halley documenting the phenomenon known as 'Baily's beads'. This event was significant in the study of astronomy and eclipses.

events.name: Rioting in England on King George I's birthday
events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1715, riots erupted in London on the birthday of King George I, as supporters of the Old Pretender, James Stuart, protested against the Hanoverian rule. This unrest reflected the deep political divisions in Britain at the time.

events.name: Unification of the Kingdom of Spain
events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1715, King Philip V unified the governments of the Kingdom of Castile and the Kingdom of Aragon into a single state, centralizing the rule of a unified Kingdom of Spain. This consolidation was a significant step in the formation of modern Spain.

events.name: Tsar Peter I of Russia witnesses the attempt of 45 Dutch and English ships
events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1715, Tsar Peter I of Russia observed the unsuccessful attempt of 45 Dutch and English ships to enter the small harbor of Saint Petersburg. This event prompted him to recognize the necessity for additional harbors to facilitate the import of Western goods into Russia.

events.name: Britain's Treason Act 1714 takes effect
events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1715, the Treason Act 1714 came into effect in the Kingdom of Great Britain, allowing for the forfeiture of property owned by individuals convicted of treason. This law remained in force until June 24, 1718, significantly impacting the legal landscape regarding treason.

events.name: Fall of Nauplion during the Ottoman–Venetian War
events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1715, the fall of Nauplion, the capital of the Venetian Kingdom of the Morea, marked a significant turning point in the Ottoman–Venetian War (1714–18). This event sealed the fate of the Peloponnese Peninsula, which was soon completely retaken by the Ottomans.

events.name: 1715 Treasure Fleet departs Havana
events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1715, a Spanish treasure fleet consisting of 12 ships, commanded by General Don Juan Ubilla, set sail from Havana, Cuba, bound for Spain. Tragically, just seven days later, 11 of these ships sank in a storm off the coast of Florida, leading to significant treasure salvage efforts in subsequent centuries.

events.name: Old Dock opens in Liverpool
events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1715, the Old Dock in Liverpool, England, opened as the world's first enclosed commercial wet dock, designed by engineer Thomas Steers. This innovative structure revolutionized maritime trade and shipping logistics in the region.

events.name: Death of King Louis XIV of France
events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1715, King Louis XIV of France passed away after a remarkable reign of 72 years. His death led to the ascension of his five-year-old great-grandson, Louis XV, with Philippe d'Orléans appointed as regent during the young king's minority.

events.name: First major Jacobite rising in Scotland
events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1715, the first major Jacobite rising erupted in Scotland against the rule of King George I of Great Britain. The Earl of Mar raised the standard of James Edward Stuart, the son of the deposed King James VII, and marched towards Edinburgh.

events.name: Daniel Voysin de la Noiraye resigns
events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1715, Daniel Voysin de la Noiraye, who had served as France's Secretary of State for War since 1709, resigned at the request of the new regent, Philippe d'Orléans, following the death of King Louis XIV.

events.name: Jacobite raid on Burntisland
events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1715, during the Jacobite rebellion in Great Britain, supporters of James Edward Stuart raided the Scottish parish of Burntisland. They captured an arsenal of weapons and began an occupation of the area, declaring Stuart as King James VIII of Scotland.

events.name: William Mackintosh lands in Scotland
events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1715, William Mackintosh of Borlum, a leader of the Jacobite rising, landed in Scotland with 1,500 men after crossing the Firth of Forth from France. This marked a significant moment in the Jacobite efforts to reclaim the throne.

events.name: Treaty of Greifswald signed
events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1715, the Treaty of Greifswald was signed between Russia and the Electorate of Hanover. This agreement recognized Russia's annexation of Swedish Ingria and Estonia while Hanover claimed the Bremen-Verden duchies.

events.name: Battle of Sheriffmuir
events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1715, the Battle of Sheriffmuir took place, where the forces of the Kingdom of Great Britain, led by John Campbell, 2nd Duke of Argyll, confronted the Jacobite army. The battle was indecisive, halting the Jacobite advance but failing to deliver a clear victory.

events.name: Battle of Preston
events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1715, the Battle of Preston concluded with government forces defeating the Jacobite incursion after a five-day siege. This battle was a significant setback for the Jacobite cause.

events.name: Third Barrier Treaty signed
events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1715, the Third Barrier Treaty was signed between Britain, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Dutch Republic. This treaty aimed to address territorial and military concerns in the region.

events.name: Nueva Planta decrees applied in Majorca
events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1715, the application of the Nueva Planta decrees in Majorca and the Balearic Islands brought these territories under the laws of the Crown of Castile, marking a significant shift in governance.

events.name: James Edward Stuart rejoins Jacobite rebels
events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1715, James Edward Stuart rejoined the Jacobite rebels in Scotland, but his efforts to rally support for the cause were unsuccessful, reflecting the waning momentum of the Jacobite uprising.

events.name: Application of the Nueva Planta decrees to Catalonia
events.enhanced_description: The Nueva Planta decrees were enacted to centralize the administration of Spain under Philip V, effectively abolishing the Principality of Catalonia as a distinct political entity. This marked a significant step in the unification of Spain and the consolidation of royal power.

events.name: Tugaloo Massacre

locations.name: Tugaloo River, South Carolina, United States

events.enhanced_description: The Tugaloo massacre was a pivotal event in the Yamasee War, leading to an alliance between the Cherokee Nation and the British province of South Carolina against the Creek Indian nation. This shift significantly altered the power dynamics in the region.

events.name: Burning of Crieff
events.enhanced_description: Following the Battle of Sheriffmuir, Jacobite forces burned the town of Crieff to the ground, reflecting the intense conflict and reprisals characteristic of the Jacobite uprisings in Scotland. This act of destruction was part of the broader struggle for Scottish independence.

events.name: 1716 Algiers Earthquake
events.enhanced_description: The 1716 Algiers earthquake sequence began with a powerful Mw 7.0 mainshock that devastated the city, resulting in significant loss of life and property, with estimates of around 20,000 fatalities. This earthquake highlighted the seismic vulnerability of the region.

events.name: James Edward Stuart flees to France
events.enhanced_description: After the failure of the Jacobite rising of 1715, James Edward Stuart fled from Scotland to France, seeking refuge and support for his cause. His departure marked a significant moment in the ongoing struggle for the Jacobite claim to the British throne.

events.name: Execution of Jacobite leaders
events.enhanced_description: In a significant act of retribution following the Jacobite uprising, leaders James Radclyffe and William Gordon were executed in London. Their deaths symbolized the harsh consequences faced by those who opposed the Hanoverian government.

events.name: Aurora Borealis seen across Europe
events.enhanced_description: On the night of March 6, 1716, an extraordinary aurora borealis was observed across Europe, from Ireland to Italy. This natural phenomenon captivated the attention of many and was documented by various observers of the time.

events.name: Charles XII of Sweden invades Norway
events.enhanced_description: In March 1716, Charles XII of Sweden led an invasion of Norway, crossing the border at Basmo, near the modern-day town of Marker. This military action was part of the larger conflict known as the Great Northern War.

events.name: Simon Fraser receives pardon
events.enhanced_description: Simon Fraser, a former Scottish rebel, was granted a pardon by King George I of Great Britain, reflecting the shifting political landscape following the Jacobite uprisings. His pardon was significant for those who had opposed the Hanoverian rule.

events.name: Ippolito Desideri arrives in Lhasa
events.enhanced_description: Italian Jesuit missionary Ippolito Desideri arrived in Lhasa, becoming one of the first Europeans to attempt to introduce Christianity to Buddhist Tibet. His mission marked a significant moment in the history of religious exchange between East and West.

events.name: Jeremias III becomes Ecumenical Patriarch
events.enhanced_description: Jeremias III was elected as the new Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, becoming the leader of the Eastern Orthodox Christian Church. His leadership was pivotal during a time of significant change and challenge for the Orthodox community.

events.name: Austria renews alliance with Venice
events.enhanced_description: In April 1716, Austria, under the rule of Charles VI, renewed its alliance with the Republic of Venice, prompting the Ottoman Empire, led by Ahmed III, to declare war. This alliance was a crucial factor in the geopolitical tensions of the time.

events.name: John Law founds Banque Générale Privée
events.enhanced_description: John Law established the Banque Générale Privée in Paris, which played a significant role in the financial system of France. His banking innovations were pivotal in the development of modern financial practices.

events.name: Formation of artillery companies
events.enhanced_description: By Royal Warrant of King George I, two companies of field artillery were raised in Woolwich, each comprising 100 men. This formation was part of the ongoing military reforms in Britain during the early 18th century.

events.name: Duke of Marlborough suffers stroke
events.enhanced_description: John Churchill, the 1st Duke of Marlborough, suffered a paralytic stroke, marking a significant decline in the health of one of Britain's most celebrated military leaders. His condition affected the political and military landscape of the time.

events.name: Execution of Sikh Khalsa members
events.enhanced_description: In a brutal crackdown, 600 imprisoned members of the failed Sikh Khalsa rebellion against the Mughal Empire were executed on the orders of Emperor Farrukhsiyar. Banda Singh Bahadur, the rebellion's leader, faced a particularly gruesome fate.

events.name: Tokugawa Yoshimune becomes Shogun
events.enhanced_description: Tokugawa Yoshimune assumed control as the new Shogun of Japan following the death of the six-year-old Ietsugu, marking the beginning of the Kyōhō Era. His leadership would influence the direction of the Tokugawa shogunate during a time of internal and external challenges.

events.name: Prince Eugene of Savoy arrives in Brussels
events.enhanced_description: Prince Eugene of Savoy arrived in Brussels as the first Governor-General of the Austrian Netherlands, following its cession from Spain. His administration would set the stage for significant political changes in the region.

events.name: Prince Ernest Augustus created Duke
events.enhanced_description: Prince Ernest Augustus was created Duke of York and Albany in the peerage of Great Britain, reflecting the ongoing consolidation of titles and power within the British aristocracy during this period.

events.name: Battle of Dynekilen
events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Dynekilen saw the Swedish fleet defeated by a combined Danish-Norwegian fleet, marking a significant naval engagement during the Great Northern War. This battle underscored the shifting naval power in the region.

events.name: Siege of Corfu
events.enhanced_description: On August 21, during the Seventh Ottoman-Venetian War, the Ottoman Empire laid siege to Corfu, the last bastion of the Republic of Venice in the Greek islands. The siege ultimately failed, preserving Venetian control over the island.

events.name: Founding of Natchez
events.enhanced_description: Natchez, one of the oldest towns on the Mississippi River, was founded by French civilians at the site of Fort Rosalie. This establishment marked an important development in the French colonial presence in North America.

events.name: George Seton escapes from Tower of London

locations.name: Tower of London, London, England, United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: George Seton, the 5th Earl of Winton, escaped from the Tower of London, where he was under sentence of death for his involvement in the Jacobite rising of 1715. His flight into exile underscored the ongoing tensions between Jacobites and the Hanoverian government.

events.name: Battle of Petrovaradin
events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Petrovaradin, 83,300 Austrian troops under Prince Eugene of Savoy defeated 150,000 Ottoman Turks led by Silahdar Damat Ali Pasha, who was killed in the battle. This victory was a significant moment in the ongoing conflict between the Habsburg Monarchy and the Ottoman Empire.

events.name: Charles VI returns from Italy
events.enhanced_description: Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor, returned to Vienna from Italy, marking a significant moment in his reign as he navigated the complex political landscape of Europe during the early 18th century.

events.name: Maria's Rebellion
events.enhanced_description: In September 1716, Maria, an enslaved African woman on the Dutch West India Company's plantation in Curaçao, revolted against her overseer, Christiaan Muller, killing him and several members of his family. The rebellion lasted ten days before it was suppressed, leading to Maria's execution by burning at the stake on November 9, 1716.

events.name: Alexei Petrovich's Flight
events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1716, Alexei Petrovich, the Tsarevich of Russia and son of Tsar Peter the Great, fled Saint Petersburg with his mistress and several companions. After spending over a year in Austria, he returned to Russia, where he was arrested and ultimately died in prison in 1718.

events.name: Siege of Temeșvar
events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Temeșvar, which lasted six weeks, concluded on October 12, 1716, when the Ottoman defenders surrendered to the Austrian forces led by Prince Eugene of Savoy. This marked a significant territorial gain for the Habsburg Empire, as the Turks were forced to leave behind their artillery and relinquish claims to Hungary.

events.name: Laws Against Jacobites
events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1716, two significant laws were enacted in the Highlands of Scotland aimed at curbing the influence of Jacobites who sought to restore the House of Stuart. The Disarming Act restricted the carrying of weapons, while amendments to the Treason Act allowed for broader jurisdiction in treason trials.

events.name: Wapping Fire
events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1716, a devastating fire broke out in Wapping, London, resulting in the deaths of fifty people and the destruction of 150 houses. This incident followed closely on the heels of another fire at the Spring Gardens, highlighting the ongoing challenges of fire safety in urban areas.

events.name: Charles Townshend's Demotion
events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1716, Charles Townshend, 2nd Viscount Townshend, was demoted from his position as Secretary of State for the Northern Department in the British government, with James Stanhope taking his place. This event was a precursor to the Whig Split of 1717, indicating shifting political alliances.

events.name: Blackbeard's Command
events.enhanced_description: In 1716, the notorious English pirate Edward Teach, better known as Blackbeard, was given command of a sloop in the Bahamas. His leadership marked a significant moment in the Golden Age of Piracy, as he became one of the most feared pirates of the Caribbean.

events.name: Peter the Great Studies Medicine
